newsitem.title: NORWAY: U.S. troops could return to Bosnia - Perry.
newsitem.headline: U.S. troops could return to Bosnia - Perry.

text.p: U.S. Defence Secretary William Perry, under pressure from the NATO allies, said on Thursday that Washington would consider sending U.S. troops back into Bosnia next year if the alliance deemed it necessary.
"I realise that many allies have said that they would only participate in a follow-on force if the United States participated," he said at a meeting of alliance defence ministers.
The meeting had ordered a study of missions and risks of any new NATO-led force in Bosnia next year to take over from the current international peace implementation force (IFOR).

"The United States is not prepared to make a commitment at this time, but we are prepared to consider participating if the NATO study shows that our involvement is necessary and appropriate," Perry told a news conference.

France, Germany, Denmark and Norway have virtually promised participation in any new military force replacing the current 52-000-member IFOR force scheduled to leave troubled Bosnia in late December. Russia has also expressed strong interest.
But the United States, with 15,000 troops in the current force, has been reluctant to make any decision until the mission is fully defined.
Commitment to such a force could be a risky political move for incumbent President Bill Clinton ahead of the November 5 U.S. presidential election.

Perry said the Clinton administration would consult Congress over the decision and several missions would be considered for a new force, including simply preventing war or a more expanded "stabilisation" of the current shaky peace in Bosnia.

Stabilisation could focus on duties such as guaranteeing freedom of movement for civilians in Bosnia, Perry said. But preventing war would require a simpler plan such as using warplanes and waiting with troops "over the horizon" outside of Bosnia to keep the factions from starting a new war, he told reporters.
But Perry, who earlier urged ministers at the two-day meeting not to turn soldiers into a Bosnia police force, refused to take an immediate position on what a new military force should do.
"I do not want at this time to express a personal view, or certainly for that matter a United States view, on which of those missions is preferred," he said.

"I want to see what the findings are from the military authorities, what the recommendations are from the Council (the North Atlantic Council of NATO). At that time, I will be prepared to make a recommendation to the President. But I am not at this time."

But Perry stressed that whatever the mission, that any follow-on force should have a clear statement of tasks to be accomplished, a strong force appropriate to those tasks and "robust rules of engagement."

On another issue, Perry said the United States favoured reorganising NATO's military command structure to give a higher profile to European participation in the wake of an announced French decision to re-enter the military structure of the alliance.

But Perry conceded that Washington and Paris remained at odds over France's demand that a European officer replace the traditional U.S. commander of southern NATO forces based in Naples, Italy. Washington, he said, insisted that an American officer remain in charge.

"It is quite clear we have a different view on that issue," he said, adding that the Pentagon felt it essential that NATO's AFSOUTH (Allied Forces South) command, which includes the U.S. Sixth Fleet and other forces in the Mediterranean, remain under U.S. leadership.
"It makes supreme military sense to put an American commander in charge," he told reporters. "We must protect what works and change what doesn't work -- not the other way around."
